messages.author: 5baa09ab3ebac9af
messages.subject: Consult about model fit and % CV
parts:
Hello Distance-Sampling list,

I am new to Distance and I am analyzing point-transect data for multiple
bird species. I calculated overall detection function and ran 2 analysis
using a suite of 5 models for each. In the first analysis the best model was
the hazard-rate / cosine, and it gave good fit (I can see a slight shoulder)
but the %CV are high (29 -32%). For the second analysis, the Uniform /
Cosine was the best model, and the %CV dropped substantially (10-16%). I
looked at the results and both produced similar density estimates.

I would like to ask in these 2 scenarios, if you would recommend to keep the
models with lower %CV and not very good fit, or the other with better fit
but high CV%. I apologize if this seems too obvious.

Thanks,

Carolina

messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: Consult about model fit and % CV
parts:
Carolina:

There is a considerable amount of discussion about model selection on
various list-servers including this one. Those discussions involve a
variety of metrics, many involving information-theoretic measures.
Recognise the information-theoretic measures assess relative fit (i.e.,
comparing models within a set). Those metrics should be used in
conjunction with an absolute measure of fit (such as the goodness of fit
tests found in Distance) to get a complete picture of the model most
appropriate for your data.

In your second paragraph you describe a nice example of the
bias-precision tradeoff. In your first situation you have high
precision (low CV) and high bias (poor fit); whereas in your second
situation you have lower precision (high CV) and smaller bias (better fit).

The hazard rate key function uses more parameters to fit the detection
function and as a consequence is capable of fitting a greater universe
of data shapes. The cost of having this additional flexibility is
spreading your precious data across a greater number of parameters, and
hence estimating those parameters with poorer precision.

I would rather have a result that on average is correct (low bias) but
with lower precision that acknowledges I am not as smart as I wish I was
(imprecise). I stand a better chance of my confidence intervals
including the true population size in this case.
